nameStory: The 'broad-footed' part of this bee's name comes from its notably wide tarsi - the foot-like segments at the end of its legs that help it grip surfaces while foraging. The 'cellophane' name comes from the thin, transparent, plastic-like material these bees secrete to line their underground nest cells, which feels smooth and waterproof to the touch.
description: The Broad-footed Cellophane Bee is a solitary ground-nesting bee that's part of the plasterer bee family. These medium-sized bees are skilled excavators, digging burrows in bare or sparsely vegetated soil where females raise their young in individual cells. Like other cellophane bees, they're important native pollinators that emerge at specific times to match the blooming of their preferred flowers. You'll recognize them by their relatively robust build and the distinctive wide 'feet' that give them their name.

idTips.label: Broad tarsi
idTips.description: The feet (tarsi) are noticeably wider than those of other similar bees, appearing almost paddle-like when viewed closely - this is the bee's signature feature

idTips.label: Ground nesting behavior
idTips.description: Watch for bees flying low over bare ground or emerging from small holes in sandy or clay soil, often creating little mounds of excavated dirt

idTips.label: Solitary activity
idTips.description: Unlike social bees, you'll see individuals working alone, though multiple females may nest in the same favorable area

idTips.label: Robust build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a sturdy, somewhat fuzzy body that appears well-built for digging and carrying pollen loads

idTips.label: Specialized foraging
idTips.description: Often seen visiting specific flower types during their active period, showing strong preference for particular plant species

habitat: Look for Broad-footed Cellophane Bees in areas with exposed, well-drained soil such as sandy banks, clay slopes, or sparse grasslands where they can easily excavate their nests. They prefer sites with minimal vegetation cover and good sun exposure. You might spot them in coastal areas, old fields, path edges, or even disturbed urban soils where conditions are right for digging.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering and begin excavating nests in suitable soil, with females actively digging and provisioning cells with pollen balls.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you're most likely to see adults foraging on flowers and working at nest sites, with new generation developing underground.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down as the new generation completes development but remains in sealed cells, preparing to overwinter until next spring.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity above ground - the next generation rests in sealed underground cells, surviving freezing temperatures in their waterproof cellophane-lined chambers.

funFact: These bees are nature's plastic manufacturers - they actually produce their own biodegradable 'cellophane' by secreting a polymer from special glands, then spread it with their tongues to waterproof their nest cells, creating a technique that predates human plastic invention by millions of years!
confusionNotes: With 12 different cellophane bee species in New England, distinguishing them can be tricky without close examination. The key memory trick is in the name - look for those distinctively broad, paddle-like feet that set this species apart from its more narrow-footed cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'cellophane bee,' these native insects have no relation to the synthetic cellophane material invented in the early 1900s - they were creating their own transparent, waterproof nest linings millions of years before humans discovered plastic-making techniques.
compareHints: Among New England's dozen cellophane bee species, the Broad-footed stands out with its notably wide tarsi, while species like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee or Aster Cellophane Bee are named for their flower preferences rather than physical features. The Blueberry Cellophane Bee tends to be more specialized in habitat, whereas the Broad-footed is more generalized in its nesting site selection.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cellophane bees, the Unequal Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its preference for early spring tree blossoms, especially maples and willows, while relatives like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee specialize in late-season flowers.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the rufous-backed stands out for its prominent rusty-red thoracic hair, while most relatives like the unequal cellophane bee have more subdued brown or gray coloring.
Among New England's cellophane bees, the Spine-shouldered stands out primarily due to its namesake shoulder spines, which most relatives lack.

Unlike the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee which specializes on late-summer flowers, or the Aster Cellophane Bee found on fall composites, the Blueberry Cellophane Bee is strictly a spring specialist of heath family plants.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the Aster Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its late-season activity and aster specialization, while the Unequal Cellophane Bee flies much earlier in spring when fruit trees bloom.
